marrow__ANAT_CH40_Q002.takeaway: Pectoralis minor crosses the axillary artery and divides it into first, second and third parts.
marrow__ANAT_CH40_Q002.displayText: The axillary artery is divided into three parts by the pectoralis minor muscle. It is the continuation of the subclavian artery from the outer border of the first rib to the lower border of teres major, after which it becomes the brachial artery. The source table shows the relation of each part to pectoralis minor and its branches.
emphasis: The axillary artery is divided into three parts by the pectoralis minor muscle
It is the continuation of the subclavian artery from the outer border of the first rib to the lower border of teres major, after which it becomes the brachial artery
The source table shows the relation of each part to pectoralis minor and its branches

rationales.a: Pectoralis major overlies the artery but does not define its three parts.
rationales.b: Teres major marks the inferior transition of axillary artery into brachial artery, not the three-part division.
rationales.d: Teres minor is not the landmark dividing the axillary artery.

marrow__ANAT_CH40_Q003.displayText: Scapular anastomosis preserves upper-limb circulation when the axillary artery is interrupted. The source states that the key anastomosis occurs between branches of the first part of the subclavian artery and branches of the third part of the axillary artery, with additional anastomoses among intercostal arteries. The source diagram and table show the scapular and acromial networks.

marrow__ANAT_CH40_Q004.takeaway: The anterior/posterior circumflex humeral vessels around the surgical neck branch from the third part of the axillary artery.
marrow__ANAT_CH40_Q004.displayText: Branches of the third part of the axillary artery supply the surgical-neck region of the humerus. The source names the anterior circumflex humeral, posterior circumflex humeral and subscapular arteries, noting that the subscapular artery is not involved in the local anastomosis. A surgical-neck fracture can injure the posterior circumflex humeral artery and accompanying axillary nerve; positional compression can also occur in throwing athletes.

marrow__ANAT_CH40_Q005.displayText: The anterior circumflex humeral artery is a branch of the axillary artery and therefore is not expected to show decreased flow from a brachial-artery blockage. The source lists brachial branches including profunda brachii, anterior descending (radial collateral), posterior descending (middle collateral), superior ulnar collateral and inferior ulnar collateral arteries.

marrow__ANAT_CH40_Q006.displayText: The interosseous recurrent artery is a branch of the posterior interosseous artery. The posterior interosseous artery originates from the common interosseous branch of the ulnar artery and contributes a recurrent interosseous artery to the vascular network around the elbow.

Distally it perforates the membrane and terminates by joining the posterior interosseous artery.

marrow__ANAT_CH40_Q009.takeaway: A negative modified Allen test signals inadequate ulnar collateral perfusion; radial-artery puncture should be avoided.
marrow__ANAT_CH40_Q009.displayText: A negative modified Allen's test implies inadequate ulnar collateral circulation, so the radial artery should not be punctured. The test is performed before radial-artery instrumentation to assess the integrity of the superficial/deep palmar arches and ulnar patency. The patient makes a tight fist while both radial and ulnar arteries are compressed, then the hand is opened and ulnar compression is released. Return of color including the thumb is a positive test; failure of the hand to flush within about 5-15 seconds is negative and indicates inadequate ulnar circulation.

The test is performed before radial-artery instrumentation to assess the integrity of the superficial/deep palmar arches and ulnar patency
The patient makes a tight fist while both radial and ulnar arteries are compressed, then the hand is opened and ulnar compression is released

rationales.a: The result points to inadequate ulnar, not radial, collateral circulation.
rationales.b: This option also misidentifies the deficient circulation as radial.
rationales.c: With inadequate ulnar perfusion, radial puncture is unsafe rather than the preferred action.

marrow__ANAT_CH40_Q010.takeaway: An AV fistula provides the high venous flow needed for dialysis; the source gives a target range of roughly 250–500 mL/min.
marrow__ANAT_CH40_Q010.displayText: Hemodialysis requires substantial flow; the source states approximately 250-500 mL/min. Because peripheral veins do not normally provide such high flow, an arteriovenous fistula is created. The source lists two examples: radial artery to cephalic vein at the wrist (most common) and brachial artery to cephalic vein at the elbow.

marrow__ANAT_CH40_Q011.takeaway: The palmar venous network gives rise to the median antebrachial vein; dorsal venous network gives cephalic and basilic veins.
marrow__ANAT_CH40_Q011.displayText: The palmar venous network gives rise to the median antebrachial vein. This is a superficial vein of the anterior forearm; it drains superficial structures of the forearm and wrist and ascends toward the cubital fossa, where it may divide into median cephalic and median basilic veins in an inverted Y configuration. The dorsal venous network gives rise to the cephalic and basilic veins.
emphasis: The palmar venous network gives rise to the median antebrachial vein

rationales.a: Cephalic vein is associated with the dorsal venous network on the preaxial side.
rationales.b: Basilic vein also arises from the dorsal venous network on the postaxial side.
rationales.d: Median cubital vein is a connecting channel at the cubital fossa, not the direct continuation from palmar venous network.

marrow__ANAT_CH40_Q012.takeaway: The median cubital (antecubital) vein is superficial and accessible over the bicipital aponeurosis, making it preferred for venipuncture.
marrow__ANAT_CH40_Q012.displayText: The antecubital vein (median cubital vein) is the preferred vein for direct blood sampling. The source notes that it connects the cephalic and basilic veins at the roof of the cubital fossa, lies superficial to the bicipital aponeurosis and is readily accessible. It is also used for IV injections, blood transfusions and blood withdrawal. The source reviews the cephalic, basilic and brachial veins as alternatives/anatomical relations.

rationales.a: Cephalic vein is a possible access vein but is not the preferred accessible cubital connection described.
rationales.c: Basilic vein is an alternative but is closer to the medial neurovascular structures.
rationales.d: Brachial veins are deep venae comitantes and are not the routine superficial sampling site.

marrow__ANAT_CH40_Q013.displayText: The cephalic vein drains into the axillary vein. The source describes two routes: direct drainage after piercing the clavipectoral fascia, and a smaller amount through the median cubital vein into the basilic vein and then the axillary vein.

rationales.b: The cephalic vein typically enters axillary vein before the latter becomes subclavian at the first rib.
rationales.d: Basilic may receive an alternate communicating route but is not the direct destination of cephalic vein.

marrow__ANAT_CH40_Q014.takeaway: Cephalic vein runs along the radial/preaxial border of the upper limb; basilic is postaxial/ulnar.
marrow__ANAT_CH40_Q014.displayText: The cephalic vein is a pre-axial vein. Pre-axial and post-axial borders are named according to their position relative to the limb axis. In the adult upper limb the radial/outer border is pre-axial and carries the cephalic vein, while the ulnar/inner border is post-axial and carries the basilic vein.

rationales.b: Basilic vein is the postaxial vein along the ulnar border.
rationales.c: Axillary vein is a proximal deep vein, not the preaxial superficial marginal vein.
rationales.d: Subclavian vein continues centrally from axillary vein and is not classified as preaxial.
